messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Singificant QTLs from multiple scan but not single QTL scan
messages.body_plain:
It's possible, but I've not seen it happen, myself.

I'd more often see a single strong-effect QTL in the single-QTL scan, and then after controlling for that I'll find good evidence for further loci.

And sometimes there are important interactors, or pairs of loci linked in repulsion, that aren't seen in the single-QTL scan.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] How do I calculate residuals after fitQTL ?
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] How do I calculate residuals after fitQTL ?
messages.body_plain:
In an intercross, the additive effect covariate is coded as -1, 0, 1 for AA, AB, BB genotypes. So that's (G-2) rather than (G-2)/2.
The dominance effect is -0.5, +0.5, -0.5, and so should be (G==2)-1/2.

This is where it happens in the fitqtl code: https://github.com/kbroman/qtl/blob/master/R/fitqtl.R#L481-L491

If you have two QTL and you're including their interaction, then in the X matrix for the regression, you'd multiply each of the two columns for the first QTL with each of the two columns for the second QTL, to create four additional columns to add to the X matrix.

I think what I should do, at least for method="hk" and model="normal", is to just return the residuals from the fit.

regards,
karl

messages.body_plain:
I think I've been able to get fitqtl to return the residuals. Download and install the development version, 1.32-1, from http://www.rqtl.org/download/devel

Here's an example:

  data(fake.f2)
  fake.f2 <- calc.genoprob(fake.f2, step=1)
  qtl <- makeqtl(fake.f2, c(1, 13), c(27, 28), what="prob")
  outfq <- fitqtl(fake.f2, qtl=qtl, method="hk")
  res <- attr(outfq, "residuals")
  fit <- fake.f2$pheno[,1] - res
  plot(fit, res)

karl

  data(fake.f2)

  outfq <- fitqtl(fake.f2, qtl=qtl, method="hk")
  res <- attr(outfq, "residuals")
  fit <- fake.f2$pheno[,1] - res
  plot(fit, res)

karl

messages.body_plain:
The formula is:

  1 - 10^(-(2/n)*LOD)

where n is the sample size.  See pg 77 of the R/qtl book (http://www.rqtl.org/book).
(The 4th page in the pdf of ch 4, which is available online: http://www.rqtl.org/book/rqtlbook_ch04.pdf)

So about 12.5%:

  1 - 10^(-(2/176)*5.11)

karl

messages.body_plain:
If there are gaps > 5-10 cM between markers in the region, the evidence for linkage or for interaction could improve by adding more markers. But once you're down near 5 cM spacing, there won't be much to gain by adding more markers unless the QTL effect is quite large. You gain more by increasing the size of the cross.

karl
